title: Point location in three-dimensional subdivisions
formal: Do there exist uniform deterministic preprocessing and query algorithms that, for every explicitly represented polyhedral subdivision of a three-dimensional box of total boundary complexity \(n\), store \(O(n)\) words and answer every point-location query in \(O(\log(n+2))\) worst-case time? A query gives an arbitrary point \(q\in\mathbb R^3\) and must return the label of a subdivision region whose closure contains \(q\), or the exterior label for points outside the box. Constants are universal, the guarantee is exact, and the subdivision may have nonconvex regions.
why: Point location is a basic spatial-search operation. Resolving the simultaneous storage and query bounds would establish whether arbitrary three-dimensional partitions admit the same asymptotic search economy as planar subdivisions.
status_note: The checked 2017 handbook explicitly retains the joint bound as open. The bounded later-work review through 14 September 2026 found no resolution for the general subdivision model. The triangulated total-complexity representation and deterministic arithmetic conventions are explicit editorial specifications, rather than hidden assumptions about arbitrary face sizes.

importance.reason: A central static spatial-search problem asking whether linear representation size can coexist with logarithmic exact navigation in arbitrary three-dimensional subdivisions.

sentences: A three-dimensional subdivision divides space into labelled polyhedral regions.
After preprocessing the boundary representation, a query asks for the region containing an arbitrary supplied point.
The target is simultaneous linear storage and logarithmic worst-case query time, measured in the total representation size.
Queries on boundaries may return any incident region, and neither random queries nor convex cells are assumed.
A resolution would determine whether arbitrary spatial partitions can support exact search as economically as planar ones.

definitions: The input includes a bounded axis-aligned box \(B\) with nonempty interior, real coordinates of vertices, an embedded finite triangle mesh containing \(\partial B\), and the labels of the two incident regions of every triangle (one label is the exterior on \(\partial B\)). Nondegenerate closed triangles meet only in a common whole edge, a common vertex, or not at all. The input is promised to describe the boundaries of a partition: bounded regions are closures of the connected components of \(\operatorname{int}(B)\) minus the mesh, with disjoint interiors and no unrepresented boundary; the exterior region is \(\mathbb R^3\setminus\operatorname{int}(B)\). Arbitrary topology and collinear or coplanar incidences consistent with these conditions are allowed. Bounded regions have distinct labels \(1,\ldots,r\), with \(r\leq n\), and the exterior has label zero. All vertex coordinates, triangle vertex-index triples and incident labels are explicitly listed. Define \(n\) as their total number of real-coordinate and integer-index entries, including the box. Thus complicated polygon boundaries are charged through their triangulated representation. Any incident region is acceptable for a query on a shared face, edge or vertex, including the exterior on \(\partial B\). The algorithms are finite deterministic programs independent of the input, with rational constants, exact real registers and indexed memory. Each real \(+,-,\times,/\) operation on its domain, comparison, copy or memory access costs one step. Each stored word contains one real or one integer; query-stage integer words have \(O(\log(n+2))\) bits, with ordinary arithmetic and comparisons charged. Floor and digit extraction from reals, size-dependent advice and free geometric oracles are excluded. Storage includes the input retained for queries and temporary query workspace. Preprocessing must halt on every valid input but has no prescribed time or temporary-space bound; only the final stored structure and each query have the stated bounds.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of such algorithms, or refute it, with a complete Lean-checked proof. Existence requires constants \(C_s,C_q\) and one pair of uniform algorithms such that every valid subdivision yields a structure of at most \(C_s n\) words and every query is answered correctly within \(C_q\log_2(n+2)\) steps. Refutation must exclude all such pairs in the defined model. Expected performance, a query-distribution promise, linear storage with slower queries, or logarithmic queries with superlinear storage do not establish the positive statement.

context_blocks.text: The Open Problems Project asks for linear space and logarithmic point-location queries in a three-dimensional subdivision. Snoeyink’s 2017 handbook version states the question for a subdivision with a linear number of faces and vertices. This card makes the total boundary representation explicit; it does not count an arbitrarily complicated polygonal face as a constant-size input.

The source asks for a data structure: one preprocessing stage must support arbitrary later queries without knowing them in advance. Checking membership in every region can save storage but loses the logarithmic query requirement.

The 2017 handbook reports \(O(n\log n)\) space and \(O(\log^2 n)\) query time for general three-dimensional subdivisions, with \(O(n\log n)\) preprocessing. Its Section 38.6 then explicitly lists achieving both target bounds as open.

The same section distinguishes point membership in a single convex polyhedron and subdivisions into axis-aligned boxes, where stronger bounds are known. An algorithm restricted to those objects does not handle the arbitrary oblique subdivision boundaries in this card.

A boundary convention is necessary for exact inputs: a query may fall on a face shared by several regions. Returning any incident label avoids making the answer undefined while preserving the search task. No average over query positions or perturbation promise is used.

The target measures words and exact arithmetic operations. The finite representation and word operations prevent treating a real constant as a free oracle encoding answers to all queries; no claim about bounded coordinate bit lengths is implicit in the statement.
